groups.context:
Cinema attendance in Northland

In 2010, about 30 million cinema tickets were sold in Northland. By 2020 this number had fallen to 18 million, mainly because more people watched films at home on streaming services.

Experts expect the decline to continue more slowly. They predict that ticket sales will drop to around 15 million by 2030. However, the picture is different for young people. The number of visitors aged 15 to 24 is expected to rise slightly, because many cinemas now offer cheap student tickets and special 3D and IMAX screens.

Cinemas are also changing what they sell. By 2030, almost half of their income is expected to come from food and drinks rather than tickets.

groups.title: Listening
groups.instructions: You are going to listen to a dialogue between a radio presenter and a woman scientist who spent a year in Antarctica. For questions 41-46 decide which of the choices A, B, C, D or E is the correct answer. You have 45 seconds to look through the questions before you listen. You will listen twice only, so listen carefully. /6 x 2 = 12 points/
groups.context:
Presenter: My guest today is Dr. Helen Moore, a scientist who has just come back from a year at a research station in Antarctica. Welcome home, Helen!
Helen: Thank you. It's wonderful to see trees again!
Presenter: How many people were at the station?
Helen: In summer there are about eighty, but in winter only fourteen of us stayed. From April to October no planes can land, so we were completely alone.
Presenter: What was your research about?
Helen: I study penguins, emperor penguins in particular. I was counting the birds and measuring how the melting sea ice affects their chicks.
Presenter: What was the hardest part?
Helen: The darkness. For about three months the sun doesn't rise at all. Some people find it very depressing. We kept a strict routine, with meals at the same time and exercise every day, and that really helped.
Presenter: Was it ever dangerous?
Helen: Once, in July, our generator broke down during a storm, and the temperature inside started to drop quickly. Our engineer, Mark, worked for six hours in the cold to fix it. Everybody else stayed together in one room to keep warm. We were lucky to have him.
Presenter: Would you go back?
Helen: Definitely, but maybe next time only for the summer!

passages.title: Journey to the Bottom of the Sea
passages.text:
The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean is the deepest place on Earth. At its lowest point, called the Challenger Deep, the seabed lies almost 11,000 metres below the surface. If Mount Everest were placed inside the trench, its peak would still be about two kilometres under water.

Conditions at the bottom are extreme. There is no sunlight at all, the water is close to freezing, and the pressure is more than a thousand times greater than at the surface. For many years, scientists believed that nothing could survive there.

In 1960, two men, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh, decided to find out. They climbed into a special vessel called the Trieste, which had very thick steel walls and a tiny window. The journey down took almost five hours. When they finally reached the bottom, they stayed for only about twenty minutes, because a crack had appeared in one of the windows. They reported seeing a flat, fish-like creature on the seabed, although some scientists today doubt this.

For more than fifty years, nobody returned to the Challenger Deep. Then, in 2012, the film director James Cameron made the dive alone in a submarine he had helped to design. He spent about three hours exploring the bottom and filmed what he saw. Since then, several more expeditions have followed, and scientists have found tiny shrimp-like animals and other creatures living at great depths.

Unfortunately, explorers have also found something less welcome: plastic. In 2019, an explorer saw a plastic bag lying on the seabed nearly 11 kilometres down. For many people, **this** was a shocking sign that human pollution has reached even the most remote places on our planet.
